name: Accordion
description: Accordion is a vertical stack of collapsible containers that reveal or hide sections of content. Users can click on the accordion headers to expand or collapse content panels. Some accordions allow only one section open at a time, others support multiple. Panels usually have animations for smooth transitions.
when_to_use: Organizing large amounts of content (FAQs, menus, settings)
Progressive disclosure to reduce cognitive load
Limited screen space on mobile or small screens
when_not_to_use: Minimal content — use inline content instead
Frequently accessed content — use Tabs or Lists
Critical information that should remain visible at all times
variants: Stacked items vs. single standalone item
Plus icon (+/-) vs. chevron icon (up/down or right/down)

conflicting_elements.Select: Select displays a list of options; accordion displays content.
conflicting_elements.Disclosure button: Disclosure buttons are standalone, show partial info, typically have no container.

name: Action Sheet
description: Action Sheet is a specific style of menu that presents a set of actions or options. Originally native to iOS, now a common design pattern. Destructive actions typically have red text. Action sheets are NOT connected to screen edges (unlike bottom sheets).
when_to_use: Quick actions — simple, immediate tasks like sharing or deleting
Fewer options — best with 3–5 choices
when_not_to_use: Complex actions requiring multi-step interactions
More than 5 options
variants: Varying number of action options (1 to many)

conflicting_elements.Bottom sheet: Bottom sheet provides additional content and is anchored to 3 sides (left, right, bottom); action sheet is not anchored to edges.

name: Avatar
description: An avatar is a representation of a unique entity — like a person, a business, or an object. It is a form of account personalization and visual cue. Can come as initials, emojis, photo-realistic images, icons, logos, or illustrations. Supports badging (paired with Badge or Status Dot).
variants: Default avatar: user icon on colored background (grey most common), or initials on colored background
Shape: circular (most common), squarish, funky shapes
use_cases: Social media — visual representation of users/groups

name: Badge
description: Badges convey dynamic information, such as counts or status. Can include labels or numbers. Supplementary information attached to a parent element (e.g. card, list item). Usually static and non-interactable.
when_to_use: Status or notifications — unread messages, alerts, updates
Highlighting importance — 'New', 'Featured', 'Sale'
Compact indicators — small areas with quick information
when_not_to_use: Too much information — use labels or tooltips instead
Overuse — reduces impact
Critical actions requiring immediate attention — use modals or alerts
variants: Container shapes: pill (most common), rounded, funky
Positioning: list format, corner of parent element, embedded inside parent
Icon-only badges (e.g. verification badge, lock icon)

conflicting_elements.Chips: Chips are interactable; badges are not.
conflicting_elements.Status dot: Status dots are binary with no text/number.
conflicting_elements.Buttons: Buttons trigger actions; badges convey information.
conflicting_elements.Icons: Icons are decorative or interactable; badges convey info.

name: Banner
description: Banner displays a prominent message and related actions. Draws attention, provides contextual messages like notifications, alerts, or promotions. Usually one at a time. Remains persistent until dismissed or resolved. CTA button is optional.
when_to_use: Temporary announcements — promotions, updates, warnings
Contextual feedback — form errors, cookie consent
Non-intrusive information that should be visible but not disruptive
when_not_to_use: Permanent content — use headers or sections
Critical alerts requiring immediate attention — use modals/dialogs
Multiple banners stacked
variants: Floating, sticky banners for persistent messages
Stock ticker banners in news/finance apps

conflicting_elements.Cards: Cards display individual content; banners highlight important info.
conflicting_elements.Toasts: Toasts are temporary auto-dismiss; banners persist for important information.

name: Bottom Sheet
description: Bottom sheets display supplementary content anchored to the bottom of the screen. Users can expand, collapse, or dismiss. A drag handle may allow resizing. Extends full screen width. Two key variations: Modal (blocks interactions) and Non-modal (allows background interaction).
when_to_use: Supplementary content without leaving main screen
Temporarily important information that can be dismissed
Contextual actions tied to current screen
when_not_to_use: Primary tasks requiring full attention
Complex tasks needing more screen space
Frequent toggling between sheet and background
variants: Standard styling (rounded top corners, attached sides/bottom)
Floating container styling (detached, all rounded corners)
Non-modal / persistent bottom sheets (common with map views)

conflicting_elements.Action sheet: Action sheet is not anchored to edges; bottom sheet is anchored to 3 sides.
conflicting_elements.Dialog: Dialog requires user interaction before continuing; bottom sheet can be non-modal.

name: Button
description: Buttons help users take action. Labels express what action will occur. Consider permutations of states (default, disabled), styles (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary, icon, destructive, disabled), and sizes.
when_to_use: Triggering actions — submitting forms, starting processes, navigating
Clear, single actions — 'Submit', 'Save', 'Next'
Encouraging user interaction
when_not_to_use: Displaying static information — use text or labels
Multiple complex options — use dropdowns or menus
Overuse — use icons or links where appropriate
variants: Text buttons: standard, underlined, with icon
Types: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, Quaternary, Icon, Destructive, Disabled

conflicting_elements.Badges: Badges convey info; buttons trigger actions.
conflicting_elements.Chips: Chips are shortcuts to input values; buttons trigger actions.
conflicting_elements.FAB: FAB floats and is for primary actions only; buttons are for a range of actions.
conflicting_elements.Switches: Switches are binary toggles; buttons perform a range of actions.

name: Card
description: A card groups related content and actions into a visually distinct unit. Can be static or link to destination when clicked. Displayed alone or in groups (grid, list, carousel). Flexible size with fill or shadow for contrast. Can be borderless or outlined.
when_to_use: Group related content and actions compactly
Interactive elements users need to tap/click/swipe
Collections or grids of similar content
when_not_to_use: Simple or minimal content — use list or plain text
Highly complex content — use detailed pages or panels
Repetitive layouts introducing unnecessary repetition
variants: Container styles: elevated (drop shadow), outlined, filled color, filled image
Thumbnail sizes: large, medium, small, no thumbnail

conflicting_elements.Tiles: Tiles are for selection; cards are for displaying content.
conflicting_elements.Banner: Banners highlight important info; cards display content in collections.
conflicting_elements.Toast: Toasts are temporary alerts; cards contain detailed content.
conflicting_elements.Dialog: Dialogs require user interaction; cards organize navigable content.
conflicting_elements.Tooltip: Tooltips float above content for extra info; cards exist alongside content.
conflicting_elements.Photo: Photos are static without headlines; cards have headlines.

name: Carousel
description: Carousel is a horizontally scrollable layout that displays a series of items or elements. May come with controls (arrows/buttons). Can scroll automatically or manually. Allows multiple pieces of content in the same space.
when_to_use: Showcasing multiple items — image gallery, product images, featured items
Limited space where many items need to fit
Visual storytelling — step-by-step guides or featured highlights
when_not_to_use: Critical content that might be missed since items are hidden until scrolled
variants: Size: full screen, large card, medium card, small card

conflicting_elements.Tables: Tables scroll to show more data, not unique items.
conflicting_elements.Tabs: Tabs navigate between sections; carousels cycle through content items.

name: Checkbox
description: A checkbox is an input control that allows a user to select one or more options. Container may be square, circular, or rounded. States: selected (checked), deselected (empty), or mixed (dash).
when_to_use: Multiple selections allowed
State persistence — choices need to stay visible
Optional inputs that can be enabled/disabled independently
when_not_to_use: Single selection — use Radio Buttons
Binary actions (Yes/No) — use Switches
Complex choices — use Dropdown Menus or Wizards
variants: Circular containers (often confused with radio buttons)

conflicting_elements.Radio buttons: Radio buttons are always circular and mutually exclusive (1 option at a time).
conflicting_elements.Acknowledgement marks: Acknowledgement marks are static icons; checkboxes are dynamic.
conflicting_elements.Checkmarks in tiles: Tile checkmarks work like radio buttons (1 at a time); checkboxes allow multiple.

name: Chip
description: Chips are compact elements that represent an input, attribute, or action. Help users enter information, make selections, filter content, or trigger actions. Visually resemble a pill. Text is short. Should be interacted with. Commonly found in sets/groups.
when_to_use: Tagging or categorization — tags, labels, categories
Multiple selections — interests, skills
Compact design — small, dismissible information or actions
when_not_to_use: Complex actions requiring detailed input
Too many chips cluttering the interface
Primary actions or content needing more prominence
variants: Trailing icons: caret (filter dropdown), remove icon, number label

conflicting_elements.Badge: Badges display info/status and are non-interactable; chips are interactable.
conflicting_elements.Tab: Non-active tabs without containers are not chips.
conflicting_elements.Button: Buttons trigger actions; chips are shortcuts to input values.
conflicting_elements.Map Pin: Map pins indicate locations; chips represent content.

name: Color Picker
description: A color picker allows users to select colors from a spectrum or palette. Ranges from simple to complex. Four main variants: Color palette, color slider, color wheel, and color area.
when_to_use: Customization — personalizing content (themes, backgrounds, product colors)
Creative tools — precise color selection in design apps
Interactive experiences exploring colors
when_not_to_use: Limited choices — use a dropdown or radio buttons
Precise matching — provide hex code input option instead
variants: Color palettes: circular swatches with ring or check indicator, list/tile form
Color sliders: compact, granular control, often with hex input
Color wheels: full spectrum, more space, for precise color combinations
Color areas: select two properties simultaneously

conflicting_elements.Sliders: Not all sliders are color pickers — context matters (e.g. scale sliders).

name: Combobox
description: Combobox lets users quickly select from predefined options with an autocomplete input to filter options. A searchable dropdown with a predefined list. Editable versions allow creating new entries. Often uses Chips, Tree, and Accordion UI elements.
when_to_use: Searchable lists — filter through many options quickly
User input with suggestions — select from list or type own input
Saving space when both typing and selection are relevant
when_not_to_use: Small, fixed options — use Radio Buttons or Dropdown Menus
Complex data entry requiring multiple fields
variants: Text input search (dynamic filtering, allows non-listed inputs)
Accordions or trees for hierarchical data
Uneven input and list box width

conflicting_elements.Select: Combobox combines search+select; Select is single action (choose from list).
conflicting_elements.Search bar: Search bar finds content in a dataset; combobox selects from predefined options.

name: Command Palette
description: Command Palette provides quick access to many commands/functionalities within the app. Allows actions without navigating menus. Users can type to search for commands or navigate to specific files/sections. Usually triggered by CMD+K or CMD+P. Originated from coding editors (VSCode, Sublime Text).
when_to_use: Quick access to many commands — code editors, design tools
Power-user workflows with keyboard shortcuts
Searchable commands for large feature sets
when_not_to_use: Few actions or simple navigation
Infrequent usage of advanced functionality
variants: With tabs for complex data requirements

conflicting_elements.Search bar: Command palette is a quick shortcut window for the entire app; search bar finds content.

name: Context Menu
description: Context Menu displays an action menu related to the element that the user right-clicks on. A non-modal overlay on web interfaces. Triggered by right-click; dismissed by Esc key or clicking outside.
when_to_use: Secondary actions — less frequent actions tied to specific elements
Right-click or long-press interactions
Saving space by showing actions only when needed
when_not_to_use: Primary actions — use Buttons or Toolbar
Unintuitive triggers where users may not know how to access it
variants: With or without dividers for organization

conflicting_elements.Dropdown menu: Context menu appears near right-clicked element; dropdown appears below a trigger button.

name: Date Picker
description: A date picker lets users select a single date or a date range. Often paired with a time picker. Many variants: Calendars, Date & time picker wheels, Lists of days, Day toggles, Tiles.
when_to_use: Flexible date selection across wide range
Precise date input required
Minimizing input/formatting errors
when_not_to_use: Fixed or limited date options — use dropdowns or radio buttons
Manual entry preferred (e.g. birthdates)
Small screens where picker would clutter
variants: Calendar date picker (for date range selection — travel, booking)
Date picker wheel (specific dates or time — native iOS/Android)

conflicting_elements.Tabs: Rows of calendar dates used to organize content (not for form input) are not date pickers.

name: Dialog
description: A dialog displays content that requires user interaction, in a layer above the page or screen. Focuses attention on a single-step task, question, or message. Usually has a dismiss X icon.
when_to_use: Critical decisions or confirmations — deleting data, logging out
Requires user attention before proceeding
Focused, short, self-contained tasks
when_not_to_use: Minor feedback — use toasts or banners
Non-blocking optional information — use inline content or tooltips
Complex multi-step workflows — use dedicated pages or wizards
variants: Custom dialog with vertically stacked buttons
Custom dialog with horizontally stacked buttons
Center aligned (most common), bottom aligned, top aligned
Dialogs with text fields or other UI elements

conflicting_elements.Toast: Toasts auto-dismiss without user interaction; dialogs require buttons to dismiss.
conflicting_elements.Tooltip: Tooltips are for instructions/guidance; dialogs are for complex interactions.
conflicting_elements.Dropdown Menu: Dropdowns provide options only; dialogs contain content and require interaction.

name: Divider
description: A divider is a thin line that groups content in lists and containers. Improves content organization by separating content visually. Enhances negative space. Proper spacing is important.
when_to_use: Visual separation between different sections
Organizing related items like menu items or form fields
Highlighting visual hierarchy
when_not_to_use: Overuse in cluttered interfaces — creates noise
Areas with minimal content — makes interface feel fragmented
variants: Padding styles: center-aligned (left+right padding), left padding only, full bleed (no padding)
With text or icon in the middle

name: Drawer
description: Drawer is a panel that enters from the edge of the screen to display supplementary content. Typically indicated by a hamburger menu icon. Can enter from any side. Can be modal (auto-dismissed when interacting with background) or non-modal (allows both interactions).
when_to_use: Secondary actions not used regularly (settings, navigation links)
Limited screen space — keeping interface clean
when_not_to_use: Primary actions needed often — use buttons or tabs
Discoverability critical — users might miss hidden features
Frequent toggling between sections — use tabs or bottom bar

conflicting_elements.Dialog: Dialog is a pop-up requiring interaction before continuing; drawer is for navigation/options.
conflicting_elements.Sidebar: Sidebar is always visible and on the same level as content; drawer slides over content.

name: Dropdown Menu
description: A dropdown menu presents a list of actions, options, or links in a temporary surface. Displayed after triggered by a button. It is an overlay — topmost element when open. Anchored to the trigger.
when_to_use: Multiple options with limited space
Secondary or infrequent actions
when_not_to_use: Requires high discoverability — opt for Tabs
Frequently accessed actions — consider a Button
variants: Native iOS dropdown with trailing icons, frosted glass, light/dark

conflicting_elements.Full-screen Overlay: Full-screen overlay shows additional info/options; dropdown is a compact list.
conflicting_elements.Dialog: Dialog is for user input or info; dropdown provides selection choices.
conflicting_elements.Tooltip: Tooltip provides info about an element; dropdown allows selection from options.
conflicting_elements.Action sheet: Action sheet is anchored to bottom with cancel buttons; dropdown can appear anywhere.

name: Empty State
description: An empty state occurs when there is no data to display to users. Used to prompt action or provide input when no existing data/content exists. Without it, users hit dead ends. Types: First-time use, No results found, Post completion, Feature education.
variants: First-time use empty state (e.g. Google Gemini)
dos: Provide clear context for empty state
Suggest next steps with a CTA
donts: Avoid lazy placeholder text ('no data', 'empty here')
Don't miss opportunity to educate — never leave a dead end

name: Error Message
description: An error message appears when an app fails to complete an expected action. Informs users about problems encountered during app use. Without them, users are left confused.
variants: Banner error (e.g. Netflix — yellow banner, non-inline)
Modal error (e.g. Fresha, VEED — maximum attention)
Inline validation error (e.g. Remote — red outline + text)
Minor errors: Toasts or inline hints
dos: Be clear, specific, and suggest a solution
Highlight errors visibly with red borders, icons
donts: Avoid technical jargon or vague messages
Don't interrupt workflow for minor issues — use inline messages

name: File Uploader
description: A file uploader lets users upload one or more files by dragging and dropping, or activating a button.
when_to_use: File upload flows for images or documents
Visual feedback needed — clear interactive target for dropping
Multiple items to upload at once
when_not_to_use: Limited space or mobile — drag-and-drop is challenging
Casual or infrequent actions — a standard button may suffice
variants: Standard design with dotted container, helper text, label, and button
Standard design without button (click anywhere in zone)

name: Floating Action Button
description: The Floating Action Button represents the primary action on a screen. Provides quick access to the most important function, persistently floating above all other components (maximum z-index).
when_to_use: Important CTAs — primary, often constructive actions
Constructive actions — Create, Share, Favorite
when_not_to_use: Non-important CTAs — use a regular button
Destructive actions — Trash, Error, Alerts
variants: Utility FAB (top-center for new content updates in social feeds)
Two-action FAB / Split FAB (for equal primary actions)

conflicting_elements.Button: FAB floats above content for primary actions; buttons exist in their own sections for a range of actions.

name: Full-screen Overlay
description: Full-Screen Overlay is an overlay that fills the entire screen to display supplementary content. Can only be dismissed by completing the action or pressing X. Close button should be obvious. Used when full user attention is needed.
when_to_use: Focused, immersive tasks — paywalls, free trials, onboarding
Limiting distractions from background content
when_not_to_use: Quick or minor tasks
Tasks that interrupt primary flow unnecessarily
When users need to switch between overlay and main content

conflicting_elements.Bottom sheet (tall): Tall bottom sheets never cover entire screen; full-screen overlay covers everything.

name: Gallery
description: A gallery displays a collection of items (e.g. images, cards) in an organised grid. Most common layout for visual-focused apps. Three layout types: Uniform, Masonry & Quilted.
when_to_use: Multiple visual elements — photo albums, portfolios
User browsing experience — product images
Visual-focused layouts — travel, real estate
when_not_to_use: Limited content (1-2 items) — use standalone images
Non-visual content — use Tables or Lists
variants: Masonry/waterfall layout (fixed width, varying height — popularized by Pinterest)
Quilted layout (varying sizes — popularized by Google Photos)
Small, medium, or large thumbnail sizes

name: Hyperlink
description: A hyperlink allows users to navigate from one location to another. Primary way web pages are linked. Default design: blue underlined text. Important for SEO ('backlinks'). Invented by Tim Berners-Lee.
when_to_use: Navigating to external content or additional resources
Supplementary information — 'Learn more'
when_not_to_use: Critical actions like 'Submit' or 'Save' — use a Button
When visual emphasis is needed — use a styled button
variants: Inline hyperlink (within body text — most common)

conflicting_elements.Button: Text button triggers an action within the page; hyperlink navigates to a different page/site.

name: Launch Screen
description: A launch screen is the first screen users see when they launch their app. Appears instantly and is quickly replaced with the app's first screen. Decreases sense of long load time. Often shows app logo on a solid colored background. May include graphics or animation.
variants: Minimalistic — logo only on white/plain background (e.g. Revolut, Airbnb, Headspace)
Gradient background (e.g. Fresha, Ten Percent Happier, Tinder)
Animated design (e.g. Netflix 'Tudum', Burger King, (Not Boring) Weather)
Background image design (e.g. Artsy, IKEA, Instacart)
use_cases: Required by iOS for all apps
dos: Keep it simple and brand focused
donts: Don't overlook testing across devices and screen sizes

name: Loading Indicator
description: A loading indicator is an animated spinning or dot icon that lets users know content is being loaded. Reduces user anxiety. Shows that the system is active. Can be determinate (shows exact progress) or indeterminate (shows ongoing process). May include text label or branded customization.
when_to_use: Long tasks requiring user assurance
User needs feedback that something is happening
Indeterminate waits when duration is unknown
when_not_to_use: Instant actions completing in less than a second
Frequent, short tasks
Risk of distraction or annoyance

conflicting_elements.Progress indicator: Progress indicators show measurable progress and can be cancelled/paused.
conflicting_elements.Skeleton screen: Skeleton shows a preview of content layout; loading indicator just shows loading state.

name: Map Pin
description: Map pin represents a specific point or location on a map. Used to indicate a point of interest or destination. Most commonly represented by a dot icon. May use custom illustrations, logos, or brand.
when_to_use: Marking specific locations — stores, landmarks, events
Interactive elements that provide actions or information on tap
Point of interest discovery in travel or delivery apps
when_not_to_use: Dense clusters — consider clustering pins instead
Static/decorative maps with no interaction needed
variants: Custom shape icon pins (e.g. 'P' for parking, Waze illustrations)
Logo as map pin (e.g. Taco Bell, Zara, Dunkin)
Text as map pin (e.g. price labels on hotel booking apps)
use_cases: Location-based services (food delivery, ride-hailing, hotel booking)

conflicting_elements.Map icon: Map icons (e.g. car, train) represent moving objects; map pins mark specific fixed locations.

name: Navigation Menu
description: Navigation Menu displays the primary navigation links in a drawer-styled overlay. A fly-out multi-column menu from the top navigation bar. Mega menus are upsized versions for complex websites. Vertical sidebar navigation is space-efficient for mobile.
variants: Standard link-based navigation menu (hoverable text links from top nav bar)
Navigation menu with CTA button ('Contact Sales', 'Get the App')
Mega menu with images or illustrations (e-commerce, content-rich sites)
Vertical sidebar menu variant (triggered by hamburger menu click)
use_cases: Primary navigation across pages/sections of a website

comparison.Mega menu: Best for complex, content-rich websites with extensive hierarchy

name: Page Control
description: A page control displays a row of indicator dots, each representing a page in a flat list. A filled dot denotes the current page. Best for lightweight, linear navigation with 3–7 items.
when_to_use: Swipe-based navigation — onboarding screens, image carousels
Limited number of pages (usually 3–7)
Simple, visual progress indication in step-by-step flows
when_not_to_use: Long, non-linear content — use Tabs or Lists
Large datasets — use Pagination
variants: Large solid dot (current page larger than inactive dots)
Discrete animated bar page control (e.g. Instagram/Snapchat Stories)
Continuous bar page control (no exact count indicated)
Unique page control icons (e.g. Clay app: triangle, circle, square)

conflicting_elements.Tabs: Tabs switch between views; page controls divide app into sections.
conflicting_elements.Progress indicators: Progress indicators represent ongoing tasks; page controls organize content.

name: Pagination
description: Pagination allows users to navigate between pages of content. Effective for large datasets. Should have clear page controls (next/previous, page numbers, current page highlight). Recommended 10–50 items per page. Ensure fast load times.
when_to_use: Large datasets broken into manageable pages
Predictable navigation where users need page control
Fast access to specific sections (e.g. reports)
when_not_to_use: Limited content that fits on one page
Continuous browsing preference — use infinite scrolling
High interaction cost — use lazy loading and infinite scrolling
variants: Single page number pagination (concise but no quick skip)
Multiple pages with last page shown (better UX for skipping)
Up and down arrows instead of left/right

conflicting_elements.Page control: Page control = small dots for carousels; pagination = numbered buttons for large datasets.

name: Popover
description: Popover displays information and functions temporarily in a contextual overlay that floats around its trigger (e.g. a button). Saves screen space by placing non-essential contextual information in a temporary container. Attached to a specific UI element, opened on trigger, closed with Esc key.
when_to_use: Additional, non-essential content (e.g. user profile previews)
Temporary, dismissible content (e.g. filters, actions)
Context-specific actions tied to specific UI elements
when_not_to_use: Critical information or actions — use Modal or Dialog
Frequently accessed content
variants: With caret tip (shows what element it's attached to)

conflicting_elements.Dialogs: Dialogs block interaction and require user input; popovers are non-modal.
conflicting_elements.Dropdown Menus: Dropdown menus contain only lists of options; popovers can contain richer content.
conflicting_elements.Tooltips: Tooltips are triggered by hover; popovers are triggered by click.

name: Progress Indicator
description: Progress indicators inform users about the status of ongoing processes by providing visual feedback. Two types: Progress Bar (linear or circular) and Progress Tracker (step-by-step wizard). Determinate (specific % known) vs. Indeterminate (unknown duration).
when_to_use: Long tasks showing time-to-completion
Multi-step processes to guide users
User reassurance that a task is still running
when_not_to_use: Short tasks completing quickly
Single-step, simple actions
Instant feedback
variants: Linear progress bars with text within container
Discrete progress tracker with status indicators
Discrete progress tracker with separated steps
Discrete progress tracker with even steps
Discrete progress tracker with uneven steps

conflicting_elements.Loading indicators: Progress indicators show measurable progress and can be cancelled; loading indicators just show activity.
conflicting_elements.Page control: Page control organizes content; progress indicator represents an ongoing process.

name: Radio Button
description: Radio Buttons let users select a single option from a list of predefined options. Always circular. Options are mutually exclusive — only one can be selected at a time. Named after physical car radio buttons.
when_to_use: Multiple exclusive options — mutually exclusive choices
Clear choices with enough space for all labels
Immediate selection clarity — all options visible at once
when_not_to_use: Binary choices — use a switch or checkbox
Too many options (use dropdown menu)
Complex selections dependent on other choices
variants: Standard radio button with filled dot center
Radio buttons with completely filled dots (rarer)

conflicting_elements.Checkboxes: Checkboxes allow multiple selections; radio buttons are always single-select and circular.

name: Search Bar
description: Search bar allows users to enter a keyword or phrase and get relevant information. Three levels: Global search (entire app), Page search (one page), Component search (specific component like a table). Complexity ranges from simple auto-suggestions to advanced options.
when_to_use: Large data sets needing quick filtering
Frequent user searches as a primary action
when_not_to_use: Not much content — 5-10 items easily browsable
Well-organized navigation providing easy access
variants: Magnifying glass icon on left (most common)
Auxiliary buttons: clear, audio search, image search, filter
Travel app search bars (To/From fields with location autocomplete)

conflicting_elements.Text field: Search bar is a special type of text field with magnifying glass icon and 'search' placeholder.

name: Segmented Control
description: Segmented Control is a toggle that allows users to navigate between views or select options. Primary use: organize content. Options = 'segments' on a 'track'. Can have two or more segments. When used to select options, called Segmented Buttons; when used for navigation, called Segmented Switch.
when_to_use: Few options — small number of mutually exclusive choices
Immediate switching — changes happen instantly
Equal importance — all options equally visible
when_not_to_use: Too many options
Non-binary options
Hierarchical choices where some are more important
variants: Stacked text labels (more context but taller)

conflicting_elements.Switch: Switch toggles binary on/off; segmented control selects from 2+ options by tapping a segment.
conflicting_elements.Tab: Tabs are separated items (no shared track); segmented controls have all options connected by a track.

name: Select
description: Select allows users to choose from multiple options from a dropdown menu list. Effective for straightforward choices with limited options. Shows selected value or placeholder even when closed. Commonly used in form submission.
when_to_use: Limited options — defined list like country or language
Simple, single-choice decision
when_not_to_use: Too many options (10+) — use a Combobox
Multiple selections required — use Checkboxes
variants: Alternative trailing icons instead of caret
use_cases: Form submission — selecting from predefined lists

conflicting_elements.Accordions: Accordion displays content; Select displays a list of value options.
conflicting_elements.Menus: Select requires a value to be changed; menus may just list actions.

name: Sidebar
description: A sidebar makes it easy for users to navigate an app's features or sections. May include extra content or actions. Common interaction: tap hamburger menu icon to slide in sidebar. Reduces cognitive load by hiding non-core features. Always visible vs. drawer (hidden until triggered).
when_to_use: Complex navigation needs — many sections and features
Infrequently visited screens — Settings, Profile, Help
when_not_to_use: Simple navigation needs
Frequently visited screens — use Tab Bar instead
variants: User profiles at top of sidebar
Navigation rail (always visible, no hamburger trigger)

conflicting_elements.Drawer: Drawer slides over content; sidebar is always visible at the same level as content.

name: Skeleton
description: Skeleton screen displays a placeholder preview of content while the actual content is loading. Usually light grey boxes mimicking the page layout. Known to increase perceived performance vs. blank screens or loading spinners. Often uses shimmering/wave animation. Popularized by Twitter in 2012.
when_to_use: Placeholder for loading content to show structure
Improves perceived performance during data fetching
Content-rich pages with many elements
when_not_to_use: Instant content display (nearly instant load)
Simple layouts where it adds complexity without value
Frequently changing/real-time content
anatomy: Grey placeholder boxes matching content layout

conflicting_elements.Avatar placeholder: Avatar placeholder is a permanent default state; skeleton is a temporary loading state.
conflicting_elements.Loading indicator: Loading indicator is a spinner; skeleton shows a preview of the content structure.

name: Slider
description: Sliders allow users to make selections from a range of values. Values don't have to be numerical. Can be circular, linear, horizontal, vertical. Discrete sliders (predefined steps) vs. Continuous sliders (any value in range).
when_to_use: Adjustable values — volume, brightness
Quick comparisons between values
when_not_to_use: Precise inputs — sliders can be inaccurate
Too many distinct options
variants: Non-circular handle with wider track (media cropping)

name: Stacked List
description: Stacked List displays a group of related content in a vertical list — usually includes text and images. Preferred over tables on mobile (no dual-axis scrolling). Provides clean, scrollable, easy-to-navigate view.
when_to_use: Ordered information in clear logical flow (task lists, search results)
Concise information per item (message previews, short descriptions)
Scannable, single column layout for mobile
when_not_to_use: Complex data needing multiple columns — use a table
Content-heavy items — use accordions instead
variants: Card-based stacked lists (distinct containers, media-rich, less compact)

conflicting_elements.Tables: Tables have unlimited columns with headers for comparison; stacked lists are single-column and simpler.

name: Status Dot
description: Status Dot is a small, circular indicator that conveys notifications or status information. Can come in different colors. Temporary — disappears when interacted with. Static and non-interactive. Indicates a binary state (active/inactive).
when_to_use: Real-time status — online/offline in chat apps
Simple, binary states — active/inactive
Compact space where subtle visual cue is needed
when_not_to_use: Detailed information — use badges or text labels
Multiple complex statuses — use icons with text or tooltips
Critical alerts — use alerts or modals
variants: Positioning: on corner of parent element
With or without status labels (e.g. 'Out of Stock', 'Recently Active')

conflicting_elements.Badges: Badges convey numerical quantity; status dots convey discrete binary state.

name: Stepper
description: A stepper is a two-segment control to increase or decrease an incremental value. Used for numbers (items, date, time). Common in e-commerce, food delivery, shopping apps.
when_to_use: Adjusting small increments (quantity of items)
Preventing invalid inputs (specific intervals only)
Simple user actions with minimal cognitive load
when_not_to_use: Large ranges or non-step values — use Text field or Slider
Fast input required — scrolling through hundreds
Limited screen space
variants: Stepper without decrement button (when value is 1 or minimum)

name: Switch
description: A switch allows users to toggle the state of a single item on or off. Active ('on') usually has accent color background; inactive ('off') has greyed background. Best for binary options.
when_to_use: Immediate actions — changes happen instantly
Binary options — on/off states
Clarity needed — clear what the toggle controls
when_not_to_use: Complex or multi-step actions requiring confirmation
Multiple choices — use radio buttons or dropdowns
Unclear or hidden effects
variants: Standard switches (native iOS style — track + thumb)

conflicting_elements.Segmented control: Segmented control text is in the thumb; switch thumb only contains icon. Segmented control is for content organization; switch is for binary on/off in settings.

name: Tab Bar
description: Tab Bar is the bottom navigation providing access to top-level destinations. Recommended 2–5 items (max 5). Often serves as primary navigation in mobile apps. Netflix and Instagram have A/B tested different tab bar items over time.
when_to_use: Navigation between top-level sections (Home, Search, Profile)
Consistent availability — navigate from anywhere
Mobile-first design with limited horizontal space
when_not_to_use: More than 6 sections — use Drawer with Hamburger Menu
Deep navigation paths — consider Breadcrumbs
Infrequent or secondary actions — use FAB or Drawer
variants: Protruded key action button (even more prominent)
use_cases: Main navigation between core app sections

name: Table
description: Tables are containers for displaying information. Allow users to quickly scan, sort, compare, and act on large amounts of data. Items in rows/columns are related. Can include sortable columns, filters, pagination. Can be static or dynamic.
when_to_use: Organizing structured data with clear categories
Enabling easy comparison across multiple items
Consistent data formatting
when_not_to_use: Small datasets — use lists or text blocks
Complex data better shown with charts/graphs
Mobile devices (especially with many columns) — horizontal scrolling required

conflicting_elements.Stacked lists: Stacked lists are single-column without strict grid; tables have multiple columns with headers enabling comparison.

name: Table of Contents
description: Table of Contents lets users quickly navigate to a particular section of the page content. Used as a navigational tool for multi-page or multi-section websites. Follows heading hierarchy (H1, H2, H3). Can improve SEO by increasing session time.
when_to_use: Long or complex articles with multiple sections
Non-linear navigation — jumping between sections
when_not_to_use: Short content readable in one go
Sequential content expected to be read start-to-finish
anatomy: Heading links (H1, H2, H3 with indentation)
variants: Placed within body text (non-sticky, top of page only)

name: Text Area
description: Text area allows users to enter multiple lines of text. A variant of text fields for collecting multiple lines of user input. Text fields can transform into Text Areas as more characters are added (e.g. Slack). Used for free form text in surveys or form data.
when_to_use: Multi-line user input — comments, reviews, descriptions
Multiple lines of content — blog drafts, code snippets
User-friendly editing with formatting options
when_not_to_use: Short responses / single-line — use Text Field
Limited space — text areas take more room
Displaying non-editable static content
variants: Outlined text area (grey border — differentiates from other components)
Text area without container (placeholder text only — common in word editors)
Text area with toolbar (older word editor UI)

conflicting_elements.Text fields: Text fields are for shorter, single-line input; text areas are for longer multi-line input.
conflicting_elements.Search bars: Search bars are for querying datasets; text areas are for free-form text input.

name: Text Field
description: Text fields allow users to enter text into a UI. May include description labels, helper text, placeholder text, and inline validation. Versatile for collecting email, password, credit card, phone, verification codes, etc.
when_to_use: User-generated input — names, emails, comments
Short & specific input — phone numbers, addresses
Flexible input with multiple answer formats
when_not_to_use: Predefined choices — use Dropdown, Radio button, or Checkbox
Long & complex input — use Text Area
No user input needed
variants: Trailing icons (password eye, camera for card scan)
Numeric-only text fields (verification codes, phone numbers)

conflicting_elements.Search bars: Search bars are a special type of text field with magnifying glass icon.

name: Tile
description: A tile allows users to select single or multiple items from a list or grid. Tiles are radio buttons or checkboxes styled with icons or images. Can have multi or single select properties. Selection indicated by filled background, outlined border, or selection icon.
when_to_use: Visual option selection — colors, product variations
Single or multi-select from visual options
when_not_to_use: Large numbers of options — use Dropdown Menus
Space constraints — use compact menu or list

conflicting_elements.Chips: Chips are compact; tiles are larger. Both used for selection/filtering.
conflicting_elements.Cards: Cards navigate to more content; tiles switch to selected state on tap.
conflicting_elements.Tabs: Tabs switch between views; tiles select items from a list.
conflicting_elements.Segmented controls: Segmented controls share a track container; tiles have distinct individual containers.

name: Time Picker
description: Time pickers help users select and set a specific time, or a range of times. Often paired with a date picker. Precision requirements vary (seconds for cooking timers vs. hour blocks for medical appointments). Three main variants: Scroll wheels, Clock dials, Select option.
when_to_use: Precise time selection needed (hours, minutes, seconds)
Consistent time formatting required (24-hour or AM/PM)
when_not_to_use: Non-specific time frames — use Radio buttons (morning/evening)
Quick, simple input where typing is faster
Complex time ranges — use a range picker
variants: Native iOS scroll wheel (most common — familiar from alarm app)
Native Android scroll wheel time picker
Tile based time picker (for booking — shows available/unavailable slots)
Slider based time picker (for start and end time ranges)
Clock based time picker (visual clock face)
Stepper based time picker (for intervals like 5min, 30min, 1hr)
Radio button based time picker (select from list)

name: Toast
description: Toasts display brief, temporary messages. Meant to be noticed without disrupting the user. Should automatically disappear. Named after the physical toaster — it pops up then goes back down.
when_to_use: Low-priority messages that don't disrupt experience
Optional user actions that encourage but don't require response
Self-dismissing messages that auto-disappear
when_not_to_use: High-priority notifications — use a Dialog
Urgent actions required — use Dialogs or Banners
Persistent messages — use a Banner instead

other: With follow-up action CTA button (bottom placement for thumb reach)
With caret tip (directional nudge — resembles tooltip)

conflicting_elements.Dialogs: Dialogs require user interaction; toasts auto-dismiss.
conflicting_elements.Banners: Banners persist and are for important info; toasts are brief and auto-disappear.
conflicting_elements.Tooltips: Tooltips give context/instructions; toasts give brief feedback after an action.

name: Toolbar
description: Toolbar provides a set of actions or tools relevant to the user's current task or view. A group of icon or text buttons. Contextual — provides quick access to actions tailored to the current context. If too many actions, put non-essential ones under an action option icon.
when_to_use: Frequent actions in a consistent, easy-to-reach location
Contextual tasks — quick access to functions for current view
Space efficiency with limited screen real estate
when_not_to_use: Too many actions — leads to clutter
Rarely used actions — use action options menu instead
anatomy: Group of icon or text buttons
variants: Vertical floating toolbars (popular in social media — TikTok, Instagram)

conflicting_elements.Tab bar: Tab bar is always at bottom and switches views; toolbar is not restricted to bottom and provides actions.
conflicting_elements.Menu: Menu provides access to wide, infrequent options; toolbar provides quick access to frequent actions.

name: Tooltip
description: Tooltips display informative text labels that provide contextual support, usually on hover (web) or on click/tap (mobile). Improve UX by providing timely, relevant information without cluttering the main interface. On web: triggered by hover over info icon. On mobile: triggered by click/tap or auto-triggered for new feature nudges.
when_to_use: Useful context — brief explanation for specific features
Progressive disclosure — explaining unfamiliar terms, icons, or new features
User onboarding — directing attention towards key features
when_not_to_use: Complete attention needed — use a Dialog instead
Repeated usage — content users already know and revisit frequently
Essential information that every user needs — put it on the page
variants: With caret tip (most common — points to specific element)
With icons (triggered by info (i) icon click)
use_cases: Form field help (guidance for specific fields)

conflicting_elements.Menu: Menus display a list of options; tooltips provide contextual information.
conflicting_elements.Toasts: Toasts give feedback after an action; tooltips give context/instructions.

name: Top Navigation Bar
description: Top Navigation Bar is the header component at the top of the screen that provides navigation and actions. Allows users to take action (search, bookmark) or navigate (cart, back button). Also known as horizontal navigation bars. Primarily used in mobile apps.
when_to_use: Brand identity or titles — app names, section titles, logo
Simple actions — Back, Search, Settings
Compact content that doesn't require much vertical space
when_not_to_use: Primary navigation for frequent section switching — use Tab Bar
Infrequent actions that clutter the area
Limited vertical space — opt for floating or collapsible alternatives
variants: Action buttons on both sides (when hamburger menu is present)
Floating top navigation bar (Snapchat, TikTok, McDonald's)

name: Tree
description: A tree visualizes the hierarchical structure of nodes / nested items. Has parent nodes (root nodes) and child nodes (leaf nodes), with multiple nesting levels. Parent nodes can expand or collapse to reveal/hide child nodes — similar to accordions.
when_to_use: Hierarchical data — folders, categories, organizational charts
Expand or collapse nodes for progressive content exploration
Frequent navigation through structured content
when_not_to_use: Flat or simple data — use a List or Grid
Too many levels of nesting — overwhelming complexity
Mobile interfaces — too much cognitive overload on small screens
variants: Tree nodes with icons and text (different icons for parent vs. child)
Tree nodes with checkboxes (for bulk actions)
Tree nodes for threaded conversations (Reddit-style comments)
use_cases: Navigation (Table of Contents, hierarchical file system)
